papers.title: Partisan Banks and Creditor Coordination Within Loan Syndicates
papers.authors: Robert M. Bushman, Sang Woo Sohn, Jianxin (Donny) Zhao
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  We investigate how firm‐level partisanship influences interactions between banks in the syndicated loan market. Because politically divergent banks hold conflicting perceptions of economic conditions, ideological distance between banks impedes consensus and elevates expected coordination costs. We find that greater political distance between a lead arranger and a participant reduces the participant's likelihood of joining a syndicate and lowers its retained loan share relative to the lead. The relation between political distance and loan share differences intensifies during periods of high national political polarization. Moreover, greater political diversity within a syndicate is associated with less restrictive loan covenants and higher interest spreads, reflecting a trade‐off where lenders sacrifice contingent control to avoid costly renegotiation gridlock. Validating our disagreement mechanism, we show that following presidential elections, banks politically misaligned with the incoming administration issue significantly more pessimistic macroeconomic forecasts than aligned banks.

papers.title: The Impact of Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation on Competitive Pricing Strategies for New Audit Engagements: Evidence From the European Union
papers.authors: Ditmir Sufaj, Simon Dekeyser, Marleen Willekens
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Mandatory audit firm rotation was introduced in the European Union (EU), in part, to make the audit market more dynamic by bringing audit engagements to market more frequently. However, it creates a countervailing economic force: By limiting the duration of auditor–client relationships, mandatory rotation shortens the period over which auditors can recoup first‐year fee discounts through fees earned in subsequent years. Consistent with this argument, we find that first‐year fee discounts decline substantially after mandatory firm rotation took effect in the EU, particularly in countries with stricter limits on auditor tenure. Thus, greater opportunities to compete for new engagements do not necessarily translate into greater first‐year fee discounts. Our findings highlight that regulators should consider not only how frequently audit engagements are brought to market but also how limits on auditor tenure shape the pricing incentives associated with competing for new clients.

papers.title: Target Firm Material Contract Redactions and Valuation in Acquisitions
papers.authors: Paul A. Griffin, Hyun A. Hong, Kyungran Lee, Jiwoo Ryou
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  We study whether and how the SEC’s confidential treatment program, which allows firms to redact proprietary information from material contracts, affects valuation in corporate acquisitions. We find that friendly acquisitions of redacting targets generate significantly higher positive announcement returns for both targets and acquirers compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. These positive returns are also more pronounced when targets are likelier to hold valuable proprietary information. In addition, friendly acquisitions of redacting targets achieve better long-term performance and recognize fewer subsequent goodwill impairments compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. Our findings of a robust association between target firm material contract redactions and target and acquirer announcement returns are consistent with a dual disclosure perspective, whereby redaction preserves target proprietary value, which is transferred privately to the acquirer through due diligence.
                  Data Availability: Data are available from public sources identified in the paper; some require a subscription.
                  JEL Classifications: D8; M41; M48.

papers.title: The Effect of Cost Elasticity Choice on Loss Reversal
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Although the prevalence of losses has been increasing over the years, little is known about how managerial decisions lead to reversing losses back to profits. We find cost elasticity choices, implied by operating actions made in advance, significantly increase the likelihood of loss reversal. We show loss firms with high cost elasticity exhibit significantly higher long-term survival rates and are therefore less likely to exercise the abandonment option than loss firms with low cost elasticity. The contributions are twofold. First, the findings shed light on a mechanism underlying loss reversal. We extend the loss literature by promoting the understanding of how ex ante cost elasticity choices affect the likelihood of loss reversal. Second, the findings enrich the cost accounting literature by demonstrating a unique performance implication of a cost elasticity choice.
                  Data Availability: The data used in this study are obtained from third-party subscription databases, Compustat and CRSP, as described in the text.
                  JEL Classifications: M41.

papers.title: Disclosing work-from-home flexibility to compete for talent? Evidence from job postings
papers.authors: Charles Ham, Rebecca N. Hann, Wenfeng Wang, Jingwen Yang
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  Job postings serve as one of the primary means to communicate with prospective employees, enabling employers to highlight the benefits of the position and attract qualified applicants. As work-from-home flexibility has become increasingly prevalent, this study examines whether employers strategically disclose work-from-home flexibility in their job postings and how this disclosure is associated with hiring outcomes. Using a comprehensive sample of job postings from US employers between 2017 and 2024, we find that employers are more likely to disclose work-from-home flexibility when facing greater labor market competition and that disclosing this flexibility is associated with a higher job vacancy filling rate, especially when work-from-home information is disclosed in a more salient manner. However, we document a positive association between work-from-home disclosures and subsequent employee turnover, suggesting potential costs associated with these disclosures. These findings add to the growing literature on firms’ strategic disclosure targeted towards labor markets.
